When something skids, it slides suddenly and without control, usually sideways or in an unintended direction, because it has lost its grip on the surface beneath it.

The two most important things about skidding are:

  1. It is uncontrolled — the person or thing doesn't want to move that way.
  2. It happens because grip is lost — the surface becomes too slippery to hold on to.

Imagine a car driving on a wet road. The driver presses the brakes hard. Instead of stopping smoothly, the tyres stop spinning but the car keeps moving forward — now sliding across the wet surface, unable to steer or stop properly. The car might swing sideways. The driver is not in control anymore.

That is skidding.

The car skidded on the wet road.

Skidding happens when there is not enough friction (grip) between two surfaces. Common causes:

  • Ice or snow on a road
  • Wet or oily surfaces
  • Loose gravel or sand
  • Braking too hard or too suddenly
  • Turning too fast

Without friction, the wheels (or feet, or any object) cannot "hold" the surface — they just slide across it.

The verb is most commonly used for vehicles, but not only:

  • The car skidded on the icy road and crashed into the barrier.
  • The truck skidded to a stop just before the red light.
  • His feet skidded on the wet kitchen floor.
  • The box skidded across the floor when she pushed it.

This is a very common phrase. It means something was moving and then skidded — lost control briefly — before finally stopping.

  • The bicycle skidded to a stop at the edge of the footpath.

It suggests the stopping was sudden, uncontrolled, and a little alarming.

These three words can feel similar, so here's how they differ:

Slip — usually very brief and sudden. Often used for a person losing their footing in a single moment.

She slipped on the wet floor. (One sudden moment — she lost balance)

Slide — smooth movement along a surface. Can be intentional or gentle. Doesn't always mean loss of control.

Children slide down the playground slide. (Intentional, smooth, enjoyable)

Skid — uncontrolled sideways or forward sliding, usually for vehicles or objects with momentum. Almost always implies something has gone wrong.

The car skidded off the road. (Loss of control, potentially dangerous)

The key feeling of skid is momentum + loss of grip = danger or near-danger.

When a vehicle skids, its tyres drag across the road and leave dark rubber streaks. These are called skid marks. You've likely seen them on roads — long black lines. They are physical evidence that a vehicle skidded at that spot.

"Skid" is also used figuratively to describe something that suddenly and uncontrollably declines:

  • The economy skidded into recession.
  • His career skidded after the scandal.

Here, the idea is the same — something was moving along steadily, then suddenly lost control and went in a bad direction. The word gives the feeling of a sudden, helpless slide downward.

Core meaningTo slide suddenly and without control, usually sideways, due to loss of grip
Most common subjectVehicles (cars, bikes, trucks), but also people and objects
Caused byWet, icy, oily, or loose surfaces; sudden braking or sharp turning
Key feelingLoss of control + momentum + something going wrong
Figurative useA sudden, uncontrolled decline (career, economy, etc.)
A Few Sentences to Fix It in Your Mind

• The motorbike skidded on a patch of oil and fell over.
  • He skidded across the polished marble floor in his socks.
  • She slammed the brakes, and the car skidded sideways before stopping.
  • The sled skidded off the path and into the snow.
  • After the news broke, the company's stock skidded badly.

Each time you read "skid," picture something that had grip, lost it, and slid helplessly — that is always what it means.
